prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms that brought frequency measurement to the 1e-18 level
for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube detector, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: B024 was first on three of eight opening ballots (Kroll, Lindroth and mine) and top three on four, the broadest support in the room. Lattice clocks are a textbook measurement-driven advance: magic-wavelength trapping removes the Doppler/recoil versus atom-number trade-off, and independent laboratories now compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, enabling tests of relativity at centimetre scales, searches for varying constants and a coming redefinition of the second. The two-name credit (Katori for the concept and first clock, Ye for taking it to record accuracy) is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. B019 is the second part because IceCube opened a genuinely new observational window: a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux, then TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane associations, a decade of consistent analyses, and early support from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD. Pairing a precision-measurement achievement with a discovery of nature gives a prize of two distinct experimental breakthroughs, both instrument-led, with three laureates in total.
statement.case_against: Both parts have real weaknesses. Lattice clocks sit in a lineage already honoured in 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems), and the SI redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so some will call this incremental or technological rather than a discovery. Halzen alone is a fragile credit for a collaboration-scale result: AMANDA and IceCube builders, analysts and the collaboration at large are not named, and the origin of most of the diffuse flux is unsettled. If the committee judges that a one-name IceCube prize is unfair, the configuration should shrink to B024 alone rather than add uncredited names I cannot support from the shortlist. A split prize also dilutes B024, which already commands majority support.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B024 first as a case where progress is limited by measurement precision, defensible with the Katori-Ye pair, and placed atom interferometry (B015) second, valuing new measurement techniques.
responses.response: I agree on B024 and on the clean Katori-Ye credit. I do not follow you to B015: the credit among Pritchard, Kasevich, Bordé and Chu is not clean, Chu is a laureate and absent from the names, and the fundamental-physics payoff is still mostly demonstrated sensitivity. I ranked it seventh for that reason and would not make it part of the prize. On the 2005 and 2012 overlap you flag, I think the lattice-clock concept is a distinct invention and not covered by either citation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B024 first as a qualitatively new capability judged by precision and theory-experiment agreement, and flagged whether it is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, with trapped ions (B036) second.
responses.response: Your precision argument matches my own, and the independent clock-to-clock agreement is what convinces me the result is solid. I take your overlap worry seriously but think it is answered by the citation: we would honour the magic-wavelength lattice, not combs or single ions. On B036 I am more reserved than you. Experimental credit is shared with Wineland (already a laureate), Monroe and the NIST group, and I would rather not choose Blatt over them without a stronger case. Two Cirac-Zoller candidates (B036, B004) also invite a split we cannot cleanly resolve.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked IceCube (B019) first as a clear discovery from nature, mature after a decade, while worrying that a single-person prize undercredits a large collaboration.
responses.response: I share both the enthusiasm and the worry, and I ranked B019 second for the same reason. Where I go further than you is in making it a second prize part, since it has first-rank support from you and top-two support from me and would be the astro-particle recognition this committee has not given. I do not think the single-name problem disappears: if the committee cannot settle credit beyond Halzen, then B019 should be the first thing dropped from my configuration, not B024. I would welcome your view on whether Halzen alone is credible, or whether the citation should name the instrument.

responses.point: Olsson ranked twisted bilayer graphene (B020) first as an experimentally original and conceptually surprising new door, while calling the single-name Halzen credit fragile and ranking IceCube only eighth.
responses.response: Your point on Halzen is the strongest argument against my second part and I do not dismiss it. On B020 I defer to you and Eriksson on condensed matter, but as an outsider to the field I see the superconducting mechanism still unresolved and the field only a few years past 2018, and the experimental credit (Cao and others) is not clean. I keep B020 as my first alternative because the reproducibility across groups is impressive, but I would not put it ahead of a mature measurement like B024 this year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B020 first as a theory-anticipated, experimentally confirmed platform opening moire quantum materials, noting that the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
responses.response: The prediction-then-confirmation structure is a strong argument and I accept that the phenomenology is stable across many groups. My reservation is timing and attribution: the decisive experiments are from 2018, the mechanism is open, and a three-name prize leaves out Yuan Cao and earlier moire band theory. I would be more comfortable if the committee can show the lasting physics does not hinge on the pairing mechanism. I keep B020 in reserve and would support it if round-two discussion settles the attribution.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen alone is an acceptable credit for IceCube, or whether the prize should instead be limited to B024.
Whether the committee sees lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the SI redefinition of the second should come first.
Whether B020 is mature enough this year given the unresolved superconducting mechanism, a field where I rely on colleagues.
Whether a 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes B042 too soon, which I cannot judge in depth.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B024. For B019 I work in astroparticle physics (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) and have no stated connection to IceCube or Halzen, but field proximity is disclosed and colleagues should weigh my view of it accordingly; I would raise recusal if a direct collaboration or personal tie surfaced.
